source: Belfield, S. and Brown, C. (2010). Guidebook on Upland Crops in Cambodia: Corn (សៀវភៅណែនាំ ស្តីពីដំណាំតំបន់ខ្ពង់រាបនៅក្នុងប្រទេសកម្ពុជា៖ ដំណាំពោត). ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
This source describes a soil-test-based method for estimating how much nitrogen fertilizer a corn crop needs, based on a laboratory soil nitrate-N (NO3) test result. The general approach: convert the lab's ppm NO3 result into an estimate of plant-available N (kg/ha) at the sampled depth, using the soil's bulk density; if soil is sampled and estimated at multiple depths (for example 0-20, 20-40, 40-60 cm), these can be summed to estimate total available N across the effective root zone. This estimated soil-supplied N is then subtracted from the crop's total N requirement (see the target-yield N requirement table) to calculate how much additional fertilizer N is needed, after also accounting for typical losses (leaching and volatilisation losses on the order of 40% are mentioned as a rule of thumb for Cambodian conditions) and any N incidentally supplied by DAP applied for phosphorus.

Because this calculation requires a laboratory nitrate-N soil test and several assumptions (bulk density, sampling depth, expected loss rate), it is best suited to extension workers or farmers with access to soil testing, rather than being usable from visual inspection alone. For most smallholder farmers without access to soil testing, the target-yield nitrogen table and the soil-nitrate decision table (see related topics) offer a simpler practical reference.
